entry.title: Google DeepMind: Building a Small Language Model

link.title: Google DeepMind: Building a Small Language Model

entry.content:
Course Overview

Completed Build Your Own Small Language Model as part of the Google DeepMind AI Research Foundations learning path. This course covers the fundamentals of language modeling — from probability distributions and n-gram models to transformer-based architectures and dataset preparation for training small language models (SLMs).

Badge:

View badge on Google Skills

Labs Completed

Lab 1.1 — Create Your Own Probability Distribution

Explored the foundations of probability distributions for language modeling. Learned how to construct and sample from discrete distributions, which form the mathematical basis for how language models predict the next token.

Key concepts:

  • Discrete probability distributions over vocabularies
  • Sampling from distributions
  • How probability distributions relate to language model outputs

� View notebook in browser · 📄 Download .ipynb

Lab 1.2 — Experiment with N-Gram Models

Built character-level and word-level n-gram language models from scratch. Implemented n-gram counting, probability estimation, and text generation using both random sampling and greedy decoding.

Key concepts:

  • N-gram model construction and counting
  • Conditional probability estimation: P(next_token | context)
  • Text generation via random sampling and greedy argmax
  • Limitations of n-gram models (sparsity, context window)

� View notebook in browser · 📄 Download .ipynb

Lab 1.3 — Compare N-Gram Models and Transformer Language Models

Compared the performance of n-gram models against transformer-based language models. Explored how transformers overcome the sparsity and context limitations of n-grams through self-attention mechanisms.

Key concepts:

  • Self-attention and positional encoding
  • Transformer architecture for language modeling
  • Performance comparison: n-gram vs. transformer
  • Trade-offs between model complexity and quality

� View notebook in browser · 📄 Download .ipynb

Lab 1.4 — Prepare the Dataset for Training a SLM

Learned how to prepare text data for training a small language model. Covered tokenization, encoding, sequence segmentation with overlapping windows, and creating input-target pairs for transformer training.

Key concepts:

  • Character-level tokenization and vocabulary building
  • Encoding text to token indices and decoding back
  • Segmenting long sequences into overlapping windows
  • Creating padded input-target pairs for training
def segment_encoded_sequence(sequence, max_length, n_overlap):
    step = max_length - n_overlap
    subsequences = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(sequence):
        segment = sequence[i : i + max_length]
        subsequences.append(segment)
        if i + max_length >= len(sequence):
            break
        i += step
    return subsequences

� View notebook in browser · 📄 Download .ipynb

Key Takeaways

  1. Probability is the foundation — Language models are ultimately probability distributions over sequences, and understanding the basics is essential.
  2. N-grams are simple but limited — They work for baseline text generation but suffer from sparsity and cannot capture long-range dependencies.
  3. Transformers solve the context problem — Self-attention allows models to weigh all previous tokens, overcoming the fixed context window of n-grams.
  4. Data preparation is critical — Proper tokenization, encoding, and segmentation with overlapping windows are essential steps before training any language model.

Next Steps

The challenge lab (documented here) applied these concepts to build a character-based Arabic language model for a real-world scenario.

entry.title: Google DeepMind: Training A Small Language Model — Challenge Lab

link.title: Google DeepMind: Training A Small Language Model — Challenge Lab

entry.content:
Challenge Lab Overview

Completed the Challenge Lab for the Train A Small Language Model course. The scenario: Cymbal Chat, an AI startup, wants to expand their chatbot to support Arabic — a language with very different grammar and character set compared to English. The task was to build and train a character-based language model pipeline for Arabic text.

Badge:

View badge on Google Skills

View notebook in browser · 📄 Download .ipynb

Scenario

Arabic presents unique challenges for NLP:

  • Right-to-left text direction
  • Character-level morphology — subwords attach to the beginning or end of words (e.g., كتاب = “book”, كتابي = “my book”, كتابك = “your book”)
  • Diacritics — optional markings above/below letters for vowel sounds
  • Character-based models can outperform word-based models for Arabic due to this morphology

Tasks Completed

Task 1 — Helper Functions and Data Loading

Loaded a dataset of 200 Arabic children’s stories and implemented preprocessing functions:

  • clean_bidi_chars() — removes Unicode bidirectional control characters
  • remove_diacritics() — strips Arabic diacritical marks to simplify text
  • display_arabic() — formats Arabic text for terminal display with RTL override
def clean_bidi_chars(text: str) -> str:
    bidi_chars = re.compile(r"[\u202A-\u202E\u2066-\u2069]")
    return bidi_chars.sub("", text)

def remove_diacritics(text: str) -> str:
    arabic_diacritics = re.compile(r"[\u064B-\u065F\u0670\u0640]")
    return arabic_diacritics.sub("", text)

Task 2 — Character Tokenizer

Built SimpleArabicCharacterTokenizer with two methods:

  • character_tokenize(text) — splits Arabic text into individual character tokens
  • join_text(tokens) — rejoins character tokens back into a string
class SimpleArabicCharacterTokenizer:
    def character_tokenize(self, text: str) -> list[str]:
        tokens = list(text)
        return tokens

    def join_text(self, tokens: list[str]) -> str:
        text = "".join(tokens)
        return text

Test output:

First line:  الشمس طلعت! بطة صغيرة تستيقظ...
Tokens:      ['ا', 'ل', 'ش', 'م', 'س', ' ', 'ط', 'ل', 'ع', 'ت', '!', ...]
Rejoined:    الشمس طلعت! بطة صغيرة تستيقظ...

Task 3 — N-Gram Text Generator

Implemented generate_text_from_ngram_model() — a text generation function that uses an n-gram model with two sampling modes:

  • Random sampling — samples next token from the probability distribution
  • Greedy sampling — picks the token with highest probability
def generate_text_from_ngram_model(
        start_prompt, n_tokens, ngram_model, tokenizer,
        sampling_mode="random"):
    
    start_tokens = tokenizer.character_tokenize(start_prompt)
    generated_tokens = start_tokens.copy()
    context_length = len(next(iter(ngram_model)))

    for _ in range(n_tokens):
        context = "".join(generated_tokens[-context_length:])
        if context not in ngram_model:
            break
        next_token_probs = ngram_model[context]
        
        if sampling_mode == "random":
            tokens = list(next_token_probs.keys())
            probs = list(next_token_probs.values())
            next_token = random.choices(tokens, weights=probs, k=1)[0]
        elif sampling_mode == "greedy":
            next_token = max(next_token_probs, key=next_token_probs.get)
        
        generated_tokens.append(next_token)

    return tokenizer.join_text(generated_tokens)

Test output (4-gram model, prompt: “يوم واحد”):

Generated: يوم واحدة. قاليوما أيته

Task 4 — Dataset Preparation for Transformer Training

Implemented two functions to prepare data for training a character-based transformer:

segment_encoded_sequence() — breaks long token sequences into overlapping windows:

def segment_encoded_sequence(sequence, max_length, n_overlap):
    step = max_length - n_overlap
    subsequences = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(sequence):
        segment = sequence[i : i + max_length]
        subsequences.append(segment)
        if i + max_length >= len(sequence):
            break
        i += step
    return subsequences

create_training_sequences() — encodes the full dataset, segments it, and creates padded input-target pairs:

def create_training_sequences(dataset, context_length, n_overlap, tokenizer):
    segmentation_length = context_length + 1
    encoded_tokens = []
    
    for text in dataset:
        token_ids = tokenizer.encode(text)
        segments = segment_encoded_sequence(
            token_ids, max_length=segmentation_length, n_overlap=n_overlap)
        encoded_tokens.extend(segments)
    
    padded_sequences = keras.preprocessing.sequence.pad_sequences(
        encoded_tokens, maxlen=segmentation_length,
        padding="post", value=tokenizer.pad_token_id)
    
    inputs = padded_sequences[:, :-1]
    targets = padded_sequences[:, 1:]
    return inputs, targets

Test output (context_length=256, n_overlap=8):

inputs shape: (X, 256), targets shape: (X, 256)

Summary

This challenge lab applied the concepts from all four preceding labs to a real-world scenario:

  1. Character tokenizer for Arabic text with RTL support
  2. N-gram text generation with random and greedy sampling
  3. Dataset segmentation with overlapping windows for transformer training
  4. Training sequence creation with proper input-target pairs and padding

The pipeline is now ready to train a character-based transformer language model for Arabic — addressing Cymbal Chat’s goal of expanding to the Arabic-speaking market.

References

  • Mohamed, M. and Al-Azani, S. (2025). Enhancing Arabic NLP Tasks through Character-Level Models and Data Augmentation. COLING 2025. Link
  • Google DeepMind AI Research Foundations
  • Previous course notes: Build Your Own Small Language Model
entry.summary: Challenge lab for the Train A Small Language Model course — building and training a character-based Arabic language model for Cymbal Chat.

entry.title: Managing Real Capital - My Experience with LSU Investment Fund

link.title: Managing Real Capital - My Experience with LSU Investment Fund

entry.content:
Introduction

During my time at Louisiana State University, I had the incredible opportunity to serve as an Investment Fund Manager for the LSU Investment Fund—a student-managed investment fund that provides hands-on experience managing real capital. This role wasn’t just academic; we were responsible for real money, real decisions, and real outcomes. The experience taught me invaluable lessons about equity research, portfolio management, and the importance of data-driven decision-making in finance.

The Challenge: Growing Assets Under Management

When I joined the fund, we were managing approximately $3.6 million in assets. Our goal was clear: outperform the market while growing our assets under management (AUM). This required a combination of rigorous research, strategic thinking, and the ability to identify undervalued opportunities in the market.

The Bloomberg Terminal: A Game-Changer

One of the most transformative aspects of this role was gaining access to and proficiency with the Bloomberg Terminal—the industry-standard platform used by professional traders, analysts, and portfolio managers worldwide. Through dedicated study and hands-on practice, I obtained the Bloomberg Market Concept (BMC) Certification, which validated my comprehensive understanding of financial markets, economic indicators, and the Bloomberg Terminal’s extensive capabilities. The terminal became my primary tool for:

  • Real-time market data: Access to live pricing, trading volumes, and market movements
  • Equity research: Comprehensive company financials, analyst reports, and industry comparisons
  • Technical analysis: Charting tools and technical indicators to identify entry and exit points
  • News and analytics: Breaking financial news and sentiment analysis
  • Portfolio analytics: Performance attribution and risk analysis tools

Leveraging EDGAR SEC Filings for Fundamental Analysis

While the Bloomberg Terminal provided real-time data and analytics, EDGAR (Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval)—the SEC’s database of company filings—became an indispensable resource for deep fundamental analysis. EDGAR gave me direct access to the source documents that form the foundation of investment research:

  • 10-K Annual Reports: Comprehensive annual filings providing detailed financial statements, management discussion and analysis (MD&A), risk factors, and business overview. These documents were essential for understanding a company’s true financial health, competitive position, and long-term strategy.

  • 10-Q Quarterly Reports: Quarterly updates on financial performance, allowing me to track trends, identify changes in business fundamentals, and spot early warning signs of deteriorating operations.

  • 8-K Current Reports: Real-time disclosures of material events—mergers, acquisitions, management changes, earnings announcements, and other significant corporate developments. Monitoring these filings helped me stay ahead of market-moving news.

  • Proxy Statements (DEF 14A): Detailed information about executive compensation, board composition, shareholder proposals, and corporate governance practices—critical for assessing management quality and alignment with shareholder interests.

  • Form 4 Filings: Insider trading reports showing when executives and directors buy or sell company stock. Tracking insider activity provided valuable signals about management’s confidence in the company’s prospects.

Using EDGAR, I could access the raw, unfiltered information directly from companies—before it was processed, interpreted, or potentially spun by sell-side analysts. This direct access to source documents allowed me to:

  • Conduct independent analysis without relying solely on third-party research
  • Identify discrepancies between company disclosures and analyst narratives
  • Track changes over time by comparing filings across multiple periods
  • Uncover hidden risks buried in footnotes, risk factors, and MD&A sections
  • Verify data accuracy by cross-referencing Bloomberg data with official SEC filings

The combination of Bloomberg Terminal’s real-time analytics and EDGAR’s comprehensive historical filings created a powerful research framework. While Bloomberg provided speed and integration, EDGAR provided depth and transparency—ensuring that every investment decision was grounded in thorough analysis of primary source documents.

Alpha Generation Through Rigorous Research

The competitive edge in portfolio management comes from identifying market inefficiencies before they’re priced in. My approach centered on developing a systematic research process that combined fundamental analysis, quantitative screening, and technical indicators to uncover mispriced securities.

The Research Framework

  1. Quantitative Screening: Using Bloomberg’s screening tools to identify companies meeting specific criteria—valuation metrics, growth rates, profitability margins, and balance sheet strength. This systematic approach helped filter thousands of potential investments down to a focused watchlist.

  2. Deep Fundamental Analysis: For each candidate, I conducted comprehensive due diligence using both Bloomberg Terminal and EDGAR SEC filings:
    • SEC filing analysis: Reviewing 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K filings to understand financial statements, business model, risk factors, and material developments
    • Financial statement analysis and trend identification from primary source documents
    • Competitive positioning and market share dynamics from management discussions
    • Management quality and capital allocation decisions assessed through proxy statements and insider trading activity
    • Industry structure and competitive moats identified through business descriptions and risk disclosures
    • Cash flow generation and capital efficiency verified through audited financial statements

  3. Valuation Modeling: Building discounted cash flow (DCF) models, comparable company analysis, and precedent transaction analysis to establish intrinsic value ranges. I paid particular attention to scenario analysis—base case, bull case, and bear case—to understand the risk/reward profile.

  4. Technical and Sentiment Analysis: While fundamentals drive long-term value, I incorporated technical analysis to optimize entry and exit timing. I also monitored sentiment indicators, analyst revisions, and insider trading activity to gauge market positioning.

  5. Risk Assessment and Portfolio Fit: Every position was evaluated not just in isolation, but in the context of portfolio construction. I analyzed correlation, sector exposure, and how each position contributed to overall portfolio risk-adjusted returns.

The Process in Practice

The video above captures one of many after-hours research sessions—a testament to the dedication required to stay ahead of the market. Markets don’t stop when trading hours end, and neither did my research. Whether analyzing earnings calls from Asian markets, reviewing overnight news flow, or updating models with the latest data, the commitment to thorough analysis was non-negotiable.

This disciplined approach led to several successful recommendations that contributed meaningfully to the fund’s alpha generation. Each investment thesis was documented, tracked, and refined based on new information—creating a feedback loop that improved decision-making over time.

Results: 16.7% AUM Growth Through Alpha Generation

Through systematic stock selection, rigorous research, and disciplined portfolio management, I contributed to growing the fund’s AUM from $3.6 million to $4.2 million—a 16.7% increase. This performance wasn’t achieved through market beta; it required generating alpha through:

  • Active stock selection: Identifying mispriced securities through fundamental and quantitative analysis
  • Risk-adjusted positioning: Constructing a portfolio that maximized Sharpe ratio and information ratio, not just absolute returns
  • Dynamic portfolio management: Continuously monitoring positions, updating theses, and rebalancing based on changing fundamentals and market conditions
  • Capital efficiency: Optimizing position sizing to balance conviction with portfolio risk constraints

Outperforming the Russell 2000 Index

Our fund’s performance outperformed the Russell 2000 Index during my tenure, demonstrating the ability to generate alpha in a competitive small-cap universe. This outperformance wasn’t accidental—it resulted from:

  • Information edge: Leveraging Bloomberg Terminal’s comprehensive data and analytics to identify opportunities before they became consensus trades
  • Disciplined execution: Maintaining conviction in positions during volatility while being quick to cut losses when theses broke down
  • Risk management: Ensuring our outperformance came from skill, not excessive risk-taking—maintaining appropriate position sizes and sector diversification
  • Continuous improvement: Learning from both winners and losers, refining the investment process, and adapting to changing market regimes

Key Learnings

1. The Power of Professional Tools

Working with the Bloomberg Terminal gave me an appreciation for the tools that professional investors use daily. The depth of data, the speed of analysis, and the integration of multiple information sources create a significant advantage over retail investors.

2. Research-Driven Decision Making

Every investment decision was backed by rigorous research and documented analysis. Successful positions weren’t based on speculation or tips—they resulted from hours of fundamental analysis, quantitative screening, and careful consideration of both upside potential and downside risks. This process-oriented approach ensures consistency and repeatability in alpha generation.

3. Real-World Application of Finance Theory

This experience bridged the gap between classroom learning and real-world application. Concepts like portfolio theory, risk management, and valuation models came alive when applied to real capital and real consequences.

4. Collaboration and Communication

Managing a fund requires collaboration with other analysts and portfolio managers. Presenting investment recommendations, defending positions, and incorporating feedback from peers were essential skills I developed.

5. Performance Under Pressure and Work Ethic

Managing real money creates real pressure, especially when positions move against you. The after-hours research sessions—captured in the video above—demonstrate the work ethic required to stay competitive. Markets are efficient, and generating alpha requires putting in the work when others aren’t. This experience taught me to remain disciplined under pressure, stick to the process, and maintain analytical rigor even when emotions run high.

Technical Skills Developed

  • Bloomberg Terminal mastery: Advanced proficiency in equity research functions (FA, GP, DES), portfolio analytics (PORT), market data (FLDS), and screening tools (EQS). Bloomberg Market Concept (BMC) Certified, demonstrating comprehensive knowledge of financial markets, economic indicators, and Bloomberg Terminal functionality. Ability to quickly navigate the platform to extract actionable insights.
  • EDGAR SEC filing analysis: Expertise in navigating and analyzing SEC filings including 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, proxy statements, and Form 4 insider trading reports. Ability to extract key insights from financial statements, MD&A sections, risk factors, and footnotes to conduct independent fundamental analysis.
  • Financial modeling: Building sophisticated DCF models, LBO models, and comparable company analysis using data from both Bloomberg and SEC filings. Experience with scenario analysis, sensitivity tables, and Monte Carlo simulations for risk assessment.
  • Portfolio construction and optimization: Understanding of modern portfolio theory, correlation analysis, factor exposure, and risk budgeting. Experience with portfolio optimization techniques to maximize risk-adjusted returns.
  • Quantitative analysis: Using statistical methods, regression analysis, and factor models to identify alpha-generating opportunities. Experience with backtesting strategies and performance attribution analysis.
  • Risk management: Understanding of VaR, CVaR, drawdown analysis, and stress testing. Ability to construct portfolios that balance return objectives with risk constraints.
  • Market microstructure: Understanding of order flow, liquidity, and execution strategies to minimize transaction costs and market impact.

Conclusion

My experience as Investment Fund Manager at LSU Investment Fund provided a rare opportunity to manage real capital in a professional environment. The 16.7% growth in AUM and our outperformance of the Russell 2000 Index demonstrate the practical application of rigorous research, disciplined portfolio management, and data-driven decision-making.

The skills developed during this role—from Bloomberg Terminal proficiency to quantitative analysis and risk management—form the foundation for a career in active portfolio management. The work ethic demonstrated through after-hours research sessions, combined with a systematic approach to alpha generation, positions me to contribute meaningfully to a hedge fund’s investment process.

This experience demonstrates:

  • Proven ability to generate alpha through systematic research and disciplined execution
  • Professional tool proficiency with industry-standard platforms like Bloomberg Terminal, validated through Bloomberg Market Concept (BMC) Certification
  • Real-world portfolio management experience with measurable, benchmarked results
  • Work ethic and dedication to the craft of investing, demonstrated through commitment beyond standard hours
  • Risk-aware approach to portfolio construction and position management

The combination of real capital, professional tools, and measurable outcomes created an environment that closely mirrors the demands of a hedge fund analyst or portfolio manager role.
entry.summary: A deep dive into my role as Investment Fund Manager at LSU Investment Fund, where I contributed to 16.7% AUM growth and learned to leverage Bloomberg Terminal for equity research

entry.title: Competing on Wall Street - TD Securities Trading Competition Invitation

link.title: Competing on Wall Street - TD Securities Trading Competition Invitation

entry.content:
Introduction

In August 2018, I had the extraordinary opportunity to participate in TD Securities’ Trading Competition in New York—one of the most prestigious student trading competitions in the financial industry. Being selected as one of only 32 students worldwide to compete was an honor in itself, but the experience of competing in a high-pressure trading environment at TD Securities’ New York headquarters was truly transformative.

The Selection Process: Competing for a Spot

The competition’s selection process was rigorous, designed to identify students with the analytical skills, quantitative aptitude, and mental fortitude required for professional trading. The application process evaluated:

  • Academic excellence: Strong performance in finance, economics, mathematics, and related quantitative fields
  • Trading experience: Demonstrated interest and experience in financial markets, whether through personal trading, internships, or academic projects
  • Problem-solving ability: Capacity to think quickly under pressure and make data-driven decisions
  • Competitive drive: Evidence of performance in high-stakes environments

Being selected from a global pool of applicants was validation that my academic work, trading experience, and analytical capabilities were recognized by industry professionals.

The Competition: High-Pressure Trading Environment

The competition took place at TD Securities’ New York headquarters, providing an authentic glimpse into the world of professional trading. The format was designed to simulate real trading floor conditions:

Real-Time Market Simulation

  • Live market data: Access to real-time pricing, order flow, and market microstructure
  • Multiple asset classes: Trading across equities, fixed income, currencies, and derivatives
  • Time pressure: Rapid decision-making required as market conditions changed in real-time
  • Risk management: Balancing profit opportunities with risk constraints and position limits

Competitive Dynamics

With 32 highly qualified participants, the competition was intense. Each participant brought unique strategies, risk tolerances, and market perspectives. The challenge wasn’t just about making profitable trades—it was about:

  • Consistent performance: Maintaining profitability across different market regimes
  • Risk-adjusted returns: Generating returns that compensated for the risks taken
  • Adaptability: Adjusting strategies as market conditions evolved throughout the competition
  • Mental resilience: Staying focused and analytical under pressure

Achieving 7th Place: Performance Under Pressure

Finishing in 7th place out of 32 participants required a combination of technical skill, strategic thinking, and emotional discipline. This achievement demonstrated:

Technical Competence

  • Market analysis: Ability to quickly assess market conditions, identify opportunities, and execute trades
  • Quantitative skills: Using mathematical models and statistical analysis to inform trading decisions
  • Technology proficiency: Navigating trading platforms, market data feeds, and execution systems efficiently

Strategic Thinking

  • Portfolio construction: Building positions that balanced risk and return across different market scenarios
  • Timing: Entering and exiting positions at optimal points based on market dynamics
  • Capital allocation: Deploying capital efficiently across opportunities while managing overall portfolio risk

Emotional Discipline

  • Pressure management: Maintaining analytical rigor and decision-making quality under time constraints
  • Risk awareness: Knowing when to take calculated risks and when to preserve capital
  • Adaptability: Adjusting strategies when initial approaches weren’t working, without panicking

The TD Securities Experience: Inside a Major Investment Bank

Beyond the competition itself, the experience provided invaluable insights into the culture and operations of a major investment bank:

Trading Floor Environment

The tour of TD Securities’ New York headquarters offered a firsthand look at:

  • Trading floor operations: How professional traders interact with markets, manage risk, and collaborate with colleagues
  • Technology infrastructure: The systems and platforms that enable high-frequency trading and real-time risk management
  • Team dynamics: How trading desks are organized and how information flows in a fast-paced environment

Industry Insights

Interactions with TD Securities professionals provided perspective on:

  • Career paths: Understanding different roles within trading, sales, and research
  • Industry trends: Learning about evolving market structures, regulatory changes, and technological innovations
  • Professional expectations: Gaining insight into what it takes to succeed in a competitive industry

Key Learnings

1. Speed and Accuracy Under Pressure

Trading competitions simulate the time pressure of real trading floors. The ability to quickly analyze information, make decisions, and execute trades accurately is essential. This experience taught me to:

  • Process information efficiently under time constraints
  • Maintain accuracy even when working quickly
  • Trust my analytical framework when making rapid decisions

2. Risk Management in Real-Time

In a competitive trading environment, risk management isn’t theoretical—it’s immediate and consequential. I learned to:

  • Monitor positions continuously and adjust as conditions change
  • Set and respect risk limits even when opportunities seem attractive
  • Balance the pursuit of returns with capital preservation

3. Market Microstructure Matters

The competition highlighted the importance of understanding market microstructure—how orders flow, how liquidity works, and how execution impacts profitability. This knowledge is crucial for:

  • Optimizing trade execution
  • Understanding when to be aggressive vs. patient
  • Recognizing market anomalies and opportunities

4. Mental Resilience

Competing against highly qualified peers in a high-pressure environment requires mental toughness. The experience reinforced:

  • The importance of staying calm under pressure
  • The value of learning from mistakes without dwelling on them
  • The need to maintain confidence while remaining humble

5. Continuous Learning

The competition exposed me to strategies, techniques, and perspectives I hadn’t encountered before. This highlighted:

  • The importance of continuous learning in finance
  • The value of learning from peers and competitors
  • The need to stay current with market developments and trading innovations

Technical Skills Developed

  • Real-time market analysis: Analyzing live market data to identify trading opportunities
  • Order execution: Understanding different order types and execution strategies
  • Risk metrics: Calculating and monitoring position-level and portfolio-level risk
  • Performance attribution: Understanding which trades and strategies contributed to overall performance
  • Market microstructure: Understanding how markets function at the transaction level

The Competitive Edge

Finishing in the top quartile (7th out of 32) in a global competition demonstrates several qualities that are valuable in professional trading:

  • Competitive performance: Ability to perform well in high-stakes, competitive environments
  • Quantitative aptitude: Strong analytical and mathematical skills applied to real-time decision-making
  • Pressure handling: Capacity to maintain performance quality under time pressure and stress
  • Strategic thinking: Ability to develop and execute trading strategies that generate consistent returns
  • Risk awareness: Understanding of risk management principles and their practical application

Conclusion

The TD Securities Trading Competition was a formative experience that provided a realistic preview of professional trading. Finishing 7th out of 32 participants validated my analytical skills, strategic thinking, and ability to perform under pressure.

The experience reinforced my interest in trading and quantitative finance, while also providing valuable insights into the culture and operations of major investment banks. The combination of competitive performance, exposure to professional trading environments, and interactions with industry professionals created a foundation for understanding what it takes to succeed in high-pressure financial markets.

For employers in trading, sales & trading, or quantitative finance, this experience demonstrates:

  • Proven competitive ability in high-stakes trading environments
  • Real-time decision-making skills under pressure
  • Risk management competence in live trading scenarios
  • Technical proficiency with trading platforms and market data
  • Mental resilience required for professional trading

The competition wasn’t just about the ranking—it was about demonstrating the skills, discipline, and mindset required to succeed in professional trading. The experience continues to inform my approach to markets, risk management, and decision-making under uncertainty.

This competition represented one of my earliest experiences in a professional trading environment. The combination of competitive performance, exposure to industry professionals, and insights into trading floor operations provided invaluable preparation for a career in finance.
entry.summary: Selected as one of 32 students worldwide to compete in TD Securities' prestigious trading competition in New York.
